patient.name: Priya Raman
patient.setting: Emergency Department, then first seizure clinic
patient.complaint: Collapsed with generalised shaking in her halls after an all-night revision session
background: On the combined oral contraceptive pill
Drinks at weekends; little sleep during exams

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' where the description of the event names the seizure type: morning jerks in a teenager (JME), staring spells in a child (absence), lip-smacking and déjà vu (temporal), a Jacksonian march (frontal), or pelvic thrusting with closed eyes (non-epileptic).

points: Priya, 19, found collapsed by her flatmate at 8 am.
Witnessed: went **stiff**, then **rhythmic jerking** of all limbs for 2 minutes.
Eyes **open**; bit the side of her tongue; wet herself.
Confused and drowsy for 40 minutes afterwards.
She had been awake all night revising.

steps.q: Priya had a similar collapse 6 months ago. Does she have epilepsy?
o: No: one seizure was provoked by alcohol
steps.r: Epilepsy is a tendency to **recurrent unprovoked seizures**, generally diagnosed after **two or more**. Sleep deprivation is a trigger, not a provoking cause like hypoglycaemia.

steps.lead: This is Priya's **second unprovoked** seizure, so she meets the working definition of epilepsy.
Stiffening then rhythmic jerking, eyes open and **postictal confusion**: Priya's event is a classic **generalised tonic-clonic** seizure.

points: On questioning: for a year, **morning jerks** of her arms.
She often **drops her toothbrush** or spills tea soon after waking.
Flatmates notice brief blank stares at breakfast.
All worse after nights out or no sleep.

steps.lead: Myoclonic jerks, absences and a GTCS, **1 to 2 hours after waking**, triggered by sleep loss and alcohol: Priya has **juvenile myoclonic epilepsy**.
Priya's eyes were open and she was confused for 40 minutes: not NEAD and not syncope. She takes no quinolones.

steps.title: Name the seizure from the story
nodes: Stiff, then jerking, open eyes, confused after → GTCS
Lip-smacking, déjà vu, epigastric aura → temporal focal
March up the limb → frontal focal

steps.text: A few jerks during a faint do **not** make it a seizure. **Rapid recovery** with a short post-ictal period points to vasovagal syncope.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (capillary glucose in an active seizure), and EEG or MRI as the tests that support the diagnosis or find a structural cause.

steps.q: Priya is still drowsy in ED. Which test do you check first?
steps.r: **Capillary glucose** first: hypoglycaemia is a reversible cause of seizures and must be excluded immediately.

steps.lead: Priya's capillary glucose is 5.2 mmol/L and her electrolytes are normal: no metabolic cause for the seizure.

steps.title: Priya's ED bloods
steps.text: Normal glucose and electrolytes; raised CK from muscle activity. Pregnancy test matters for drug choice.

visual.title: Capillary glucose
visual.label: Priya 5.2
visual.caption: Normal, so this is not a hypoglycaemic seizure.

steps.lead: In clinic, Priya's story is the diagnosis; her **EEG** shows generalised polyspike-and-wave, supporting JME.
Priya's examination is normal, but an **MRI brain** looks for any structural cause now epilepsy is suspected.

steps.text: A normal EEG does **not** exclude epilepsy. The diagnosis is **clinical**: a good eyewitness account matters more than any single test.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': IV lorazepam 4 mg for status epilepticus, then phenytoin or levetiracetam; first-line AEDs by seizure type; and avoiding valproate in women of childbearing age.

points: Still generalised jerking at **5 minutes**; IV cannula in.
Airway supported, oxygen given, glucose already normal.

visual.title: Seizure duration
visual.label: Priya 6 min
visual.caption: Over 5 minutes is status epilepticus: treat now.

steps.q: Priya has IV access and is still seizing at 6 minutes. What do you give?
steps.r: **IV lorazepam 4 mg**, repeated once if needed. Buccal midazolam is for prehospital; phenytoin is second line.

steps.lead: Priya stops after one dose of **IV lorazepam**. If two doses failed, IV phenytoin or levetiracetam would follow, then ITU.

steps.title: Convulsive status epilepticus
nodes: IV lorazepam 4 mg (prehospital: buccal midazolam / PR diazepam)
Repeat lorazepam once after 5 to 10 min
steps.caption: Pregnant with pre-eclampsia? IV magnesium sulphate instead.

steps.lead: Priya has a generalised epilepsy with **myoclonic** jerks, so **levetiracetam** is first choice: valproate is avoided as she could become pregnant.
Second-line options like **carbamazepine** are for focal seizures; it would also make Priya's pill unreliable, so an IUS would be advised.
Priya should take **5 mg folic acid** if planning pregnancy, avoid two AEDs, and know about side effects. Withdrawal only after **2 years** seizure-free.

visual.title: Priya's seizures per month
visual.caption: Levetiracetam plus sleep and alcohol advice controls her JME.

steps.lead: NICE guides Priya's drug choice; under **DVLA** rules she must stop driving and tell the DVLA until seizure-free for the required time.

steps.text: **Valproate** is the classic wrong answer for a young woman: highly teratogenic. Absence = **ethosuximide**; myoclonic = **levetiracetam**; focal and GTCS = lamotrigine or levetiracetam.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the mechanism of benzodiazepines, phenytoin, lamotrigine or valproate, why temporal seizures cause auras, or why status becomes resistant to benzodiazepines.

steps.lead: Priya's seizures are **generalised**: hypersynchronous discharges involve both hemispheres from the start.
Unlike Priya, a patient with **mesial temporal sclerosis** has focal seizures with déjà vu and epigastric auras from the hippocampus.

steps.q: How did lorazepam stop Priya's seizure?
steps.r: Benzodiazepines **enhance GABA-A** chloride influx, hyperpolarising neurons. Phenytoin and lamotrigine block sodium channels.

steps.lead: Lorazepam worked on Priya's **GABA-A** receptors. Lamotrigine and phenytoin calm **sodium channels**; valproate does both but is teratogenic.
Every minute Priya kept seizing, more **GABA-A receptors** were pulled inside the neurons: that is why lorazepam is given at 5 minutes, not 30.

visual.title: Benzodiazepine response vs seizure duration
visual.caption: Illustrative: response falls as GABA-A receptors internalise. Treat early.

mcq.q: Epilepsy is generally diagnosed after how many unprovoked seizures?
What is the triad of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy?
mcq.r: **Myoclonic jerks, absences and GTCS**, 1 to 2 hours after waking.

mcq.q: Which feature suggests a non-epileptic attack rather than epilepsy?
mcq.r: **Pelvic thrusting, mobile head, closed eyes, >3 minutes, postictal weeping.**

mcq.q: Which lobe gives déjà vu, lip-smacking and an epigastric aura?
mcq.r: **Temporal lobe** focus, often mesial temporal sclerosis.

mcq.q: What must be checked promptly in status epilepticus?
What is the gold standard for diagnosing epilepsy?
mcq.r: **Clinical diagnosis supported by EEG**; MRI looks for a structural cause.

mcq.q: What is first-line treatment for convulsive status epilepticus in hospital?
mcq.r: **IV lorazepam 4 mg**, up to two doses.

mcq.q: What is first-line for absence seizures?
Which AED is preferred in pregnancy?
mcq.r: **Lamotrigine with 5 mg folic acid**; avoid dual therapy.

mcq.q: How do phenytoin and lamotrigine work?
mcq.r: **Voltage-gated sodium channel** blockade reduces repetitive firing.

technique.stem: A 26 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department after collapsing at work. A colleague says he cried out, went rigid and then had rhythmic jerking of all four limbs for 2 minutes with his eyes open. He was incontinent of urine and was confused for 30 minutes afterwards. He had a similar episode 4 months ago. His capillary glucose is 5.6 mmol/L.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis of a collapse with movements: seizure, syncope or non-epileptic attack?

clues: rhythmic jerking of all four limbs
steps.x: **Tonic then clonic** phase, open eyes, prolonged **postictal confusion**, recurrent.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Generalised tonic-clonic seizure** (and two unprovoked events = epilepsy).

elim: Cardiac syncope is brief with rapid recovery, often on exertion.
NEAD has closed eyes, pelvic thrusting and weeping, not confusion.
A TIA gives focal loss of function, not jerking and collapse.
Vasovagal syncope recovers rapidly with a short post-ictal period.

steps.x: **B. Generalised tonic-clonic seizure.** Rule: prolonged confusion afterwards = seizure, not syncope.

technique.stem: A 42 year old woman has had three episodes over 6 months of a rising epigastric feeling, a smell of burning and lip-smacking, after which she cannot find her words. Between episodes her neurological examination is normal. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. Routine bloods are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to look for a structural cause?

steps.x: Looking for a **structural** cause, not confirming seizures.
Temporal lobe focal seizures: think **mesial temporal sclerosis** or a lesion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRI brain**, once epilepsy is suspected, to look for a structural cause.

elim: CT angiography is for vascular lesions such as aneurysms.
EEG supports the diagnosis but does not show structure.
LP is for infection; she is well between episodes.
Prolactin is unreliable and shows no structure.

steps.x: **D. MRI brain.** Rule: EEG supports the diagnosis; MRI finds the cause.

technique.stem: A 17 year old girl has a 1 year history of brief jerks of her arms in the mornings, causing her to drop things. Last week she had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure after a sleepover. An EEG shows generalised polyspike-and-wave discharges. She is not sexually active but may want children in future.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

steps.x: First-line AED: identify the seizure type and the patient's sex and age.

clues: brief jerks of her arms in the mornings
generalised tonic-clonic seizure after a sleepover
steps.x: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy in a girl of childbearing potential.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Myoclonic: **levetiracetam** preferred; avoid valproate.

elim: Carbamazepine can worsen myoclonic seizures; it is for focal epilepsy.
Ethosuximide treats absences only.
Phenytoin is not first line and can worsen myoclonus.
Valproate is teratogenic; avoid in females of childbearing age.

steps.x: **C. Levetiracetam.** Rule: young woman with myoclonic epilepsy = levetiracetam, never valproate first.

technique.stem: A 30 year old man is in convulsive status epilepticus. The first dose of IV lorazepam is given after 40 minutes of continuous seizure activity because of delayed IV access, and it has little effect. Doctors note that benzodiazepines work less well the longer a seizure lasts.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism for reduced benzodiazepine response?

steps.x: Mechanism: why do benzodiazepines fail in prolonged status?
Resistance grows with **time**, not with drug dose or past exposure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Progressive **internalisation of GABA-A receptors**, so fewer targets for benzodiazepines.

elim: Enzyme induction takes days, not minutes.
Hypoglycaemia causes seizures but does not explain benzodiazepine failure.
Lorazepam is cleared by the liver, slowly.
Nothing suggests previous benzodiazepine use.

steps.x: **C. Internalisation of GABA-A receptors.** Rule: treat status early, before the receptors disappear.

practice.stem: A 17 year old boy has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure the morning after a party where he drank alcohol and slept little. For a year he has had sudden jerks of his arms within an hour of waking, making him spill his cereal. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Morning myoclonic jerks and a GTCS triggered by alcohol and sleep deprivation in a teenager is juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.

steps.x: Diagnosis: which epilepsy syndrome?

clues: sudden jerks of his arms within an hour of waking
steps.x: Adolescent, **morning myoclonic jerks**, GTCS after sleep loss and alcohol.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.**

elim: Absence epilepsy is brief staring in younger children.
NEAD would not cause morning myoclonus.
Temporal lobe seizures give auras and automatisms.
Syncope does not cause morning jerks.

steps.x: **B. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.** Rule: teenager + morning jerks + triggers = JME.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman has episodes of a rising feeling in her stomach and intense déjà vu. Her husband sees her stare, smack her lips and fiddle with her clothes for a minute. Afterwards she cannot find her words for several minutes and does not remember the event. She had prolonged febrile convulsions as a child.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Focal seizure of frontal lobe origin
Focal seizure of temporal lobe origin
practice.e: Epigastric aura, déjà vu, automatisms, impaired awareness and postictal dysphasia are temporal lobe focal seizures, often from mesial temporal sclerosis.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a seizure type: localise it.
Epigastric aura, déjà vu, **automatisms**, postictal dysphasia; febrile convulsions suggest hippocampal sclerosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Temporal lobe** focal impaired-awareness seizure.

elim: Absences last seconds, in children, with no aura.
Frontal seizures give bizarre posturing or a Jacksonian march.
NEAD has no aura and no postictal dysphasia.
Panic attacks do not cause automatisms or amnesia.

steps.x: **C. Temporal lobe focal seizure.** Rule: déjà vu + lip-smacking + dysphasia = temporal.

practice.stem: A 7 year old girl's teacher reports that she 'switches off' many times a day, staring blankly for about 10 seconds and then carrying on as if nothing happened. She occasionally blinks rapidly during episodes. An episode is triggered in clinic by hyperventilation. Examination between episodes is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Abrupt, brief blank staring many times a day in a child, triggered by hyperventilation, with a normal examination between episodes, is absence seizures.

steps.x: Seizure type in a child.

clues: carrying on as if nothing happened
steps.x: Brief abrupt **blank staring**, instant recovery, hyperventilation trigger.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Absence seizures**: treat with ethosuximide.

elim: Atonic seizures are sudden drops.
Focal seizures last longer, with auras and postictal confusion.
JME starts in adolescence with morning jerks.
Myoclonic seizures are jerks, not staring.

steps.x: **A. Absence seizures.** Rule: child + 10 second stares + hyperventilation = absence.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man has episodes where his right hand starts jerking, then the jerking spreads up his forearm to his shoulder and the right side of his face over a minute. He remains aware throughout. Afterwards his right arm is weak for an hour. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which brain region is the seizure most likely to arise from?
practice.e: Clonic movement marching from the hand proximally (a Jacksonian march) arises from the motor cortex of the frontal lobe; the postictal weakness is Todd's paresis.

steps.x: Localise the seizure focus.

clues: spreads up his forearm to his shoulder
steps.x: A **Jacksonian march**: focal aware motor seizure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Motor cortex: **frontal lobe** (left).

elim: The cerebellum does not generate seizures.
Occipital seizures give visual phenomena.
Parietal seizures give sensory symptoms.
Temporal seizures give déjà vu, auras and automatisms.

steps.x: **B. Frontal lobe.** Rule: Jacksonian march = frontal focus.

practice.stem: A 23 year old man is brought to the Emergency Department after a witnessed collapse with generalised shaking lasting 2 minutes. He has a history of epilepsy. The witness is unsure whether this was a seizure or a faint. On examination he has a bitten lateral tongue.
practice.q: Which additional feature would most strongly support an epileptic seizure?
practice.e: Prolonged postictal confusion and drowsiness are typical after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Closed eyes, pelvic thrusting, mobile head movements and weeping suggest a non-epileptic attack.

steps.x: Which finding fits a true epileptic seizure?
Likely a **GTCS**; look for the option that matches it.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: GTCS: eyes open, fixed head, **postictal confusion/drowsiness**.

elim: Closed eyes suggest NEAD.
Pelvic thrusting suggests NEAD.
Mobile head movements suggest NEAD.
Postictal weeping suggests NEAD.

steps.x: **C. Prolonged postictal confusion.** Rule: rapid recovery = syncope; weeping = NEAD; confusion = seizure.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman with well-controlled focal epilepsy on lamotrigine has a breakthrough generalised seizure. She has not had a seizure for 3 years. Three days ago she started an antibiotic for a urinary infection. She has taken every dose of lamotrigine and is sleeping well. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her seizure?
practice.e: Quinolones such as ciprofloxacin lower the seizure threshold. Her glucose and sodium are normal, she is adherent and sleeping well.

steps.x: Cause of a breakthrough seizure: go through the triggers.

clues: started an antibiotic for a urinary infection
steps.x: New drug; adherent; rested; bloods normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A **quinolone** such as ciprofloxacin lowers the seizure threshold.

elim: Glucose is 5.4 mmol/L.
Sodium is 138 mmol/L.
She has taken every dose.
She is sleeping well.

steps.x: **A. Ciprofloxacin.** Rule: quinolones lower the seizure threshold.

practice.stem: A 54 year old man with type 1 diabetes is brought to the Emergency Department having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure that has lasted 6 minutes. His temperature is 36.4°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 152/90 mmHg and oxygen saturation 92% on 15 L oxygen. Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: In status epilepticus, capillary blood glucose is checked promptly to exclude hypoglycaemia, a quickly reversible cause, especially in a diabetic patient.

steps.x: 'Initial' investigation in an active seizure.
Status epilepticus in a patient at high risk of **hypoglycaemia**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Capillary blood glucose** now.

elim: CT comes after the seizure is controlled.
EEG is not an emergency test here.
LP is unsafe during a seizure and not first.
MRI is for a structural cause later.

steps.x: **A. Capillary blood glucose.** Rule: in any seizure, check glucose first. The raised lactate is from muscle activity.

practice.stem: A 23 year old woman attends the first seizure clinic after a second unprovoked generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Both events were witnessed and well described. Neurological examination is normal and routine bloods are normal.
practice.q: Which investigation would best support the diagnosis and help classify the epilepsy?
practice.e: Epilepsy is a clinical diagnosis supported by EEG, which also helps classify the seizure type. MRI looks for a structural cause.

steps.x: Support the diagnosis and **classify**: which test shows electrical activity?
Clinically epilepsy; now support and classify it.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **EEG**: clinical diagnosis supported by EEG.

elim: CT is for acute structural problems.
MRI shows structure, not seizure type.
Prolactin is unreliable and does not classify.
Tilt table is for syncope.

steps.x: **B. EEG.** Rule: EEG supports and classifies; MRI looks for a cause.

practice.stem: A 28 year old man with epilepsy is brought to the Emergency Department. He has been having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure for 7 minutes. IV access is in place and his capillary glucose is 6.1 mmol/L. His pulse rate is 130 bpm, BP 150/92 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% on 15 L oxygen.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Convulsive status with IV access is treated with IV lorazepam 4 mg, up to two doses. Buccal midazolam is prehospital; phenytoin and levetiracetam are second line.

steps.x: Initial treatment of an ongoing seizure in hospital.
**Status epilepticus**; IV access; glucose normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV lorazepam 4 mg.**

elim: Buccal midazolam is for no IV access, e.g. prehospital.
Second line after two benzodiazepine doses.
Second line after two benzodiazepine doses.
Oral valproate is maintenance, not acute.

steps.x: **C. IV lorazepam 4 mg.** Rule: IV access = lorazepam; no access = buccal midazolam or PR diazepam.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman is in convulsive status epilepticus in the Emergency Department. She has received two doses of IV lorazepam 4 mg, 10 minutes apart, and is still seizing. Her capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. Her pulse rate is 134 bpm and BP 158/96 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: If two doses of benzodiazepine fail, give a second-line agent: IV phenytoin (or levetiracetam or valproate). General anaesthesia in ITU is for refractory status after this.

steps.x: Next step after first-line has failed.
Benzodiazepine maximum reached.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Second line: **IV phenytoin**.

elim: Another benzodiazepine; the maximum is two doses.
Reserved for refractory status after second-line drugs.
Maximum is two doses.
Another benzodiazepine, and a prehospital route.

steps.x: **D. IV phenytoin.** Rule: two benzodiazepines, then phenytoin/levetiracetam/valproate, then ITU.

practice.stem: A 22 year old woman has generalised tonic-clonic epilepsy. She and her partner plan to start a family next year. She asks which medicine is safest. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. Pregnancy test is negative.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
practice.e: Lamotrigine with high-dose folic acid (5 mg) is preferred when planning pregnancy. Valproate is highly teratogenic and phenytoin interferes with folate.

steps.x: Drug choice when planning pregnancy.
GTCS first line is lamotrigine or levetiracetam; pregnancy planning.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lamotrigine + 5 mg folic acid**, monotherapy.

elim: Carbamazepine is second line for focal seizures.
Phenytoin interferes with folate metabolism.
Valproate is highly teratogenic.
Topiramate is teratogenic and not first line.

steps.x: **B. Lamotrigine with folic acid 5 mg.** Rule: pregnancy = lamotrigine, 5 mg folate, one drug only.

practice.stem: A 35 year old man's convulsive status epilepticus stops 2 minutes after IV lorazepam is given. A student asks how the drug ended the seizure.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of action?
practice.e: Benzodiazepines potentiate GABA-A receptor-mediated chloride influx, hyperpolarising neurons. Phenytoin and lamotrigine block sodium channels; ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels.

steps.x: Mechanism of a benzodiazepine.
Lorazepam is a **benzodiazepine**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Enhances **GABA-A** chloride influx: neurons hyperpolarise.

elim: NMDA blockade is ketamine or memantine.
T-type calcium channel blockade is ethosuximide.
Sodium channel blockade is phenytoin and lamotrigine.
GABA transaminase inhibition is vigabatrin.

steps.x: **E. Potentiates GABA-A receptor chloride influx.**

prompts.q: What is epilepsy, and when is it diagnosed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one seizure is not epilepsy.

points.p: Tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures
points.why: Provoked seizures (hypoglycaemia, alcohol withdrawal) are not epilepsy.

points.p: Diagnosed after two or more unprovoked seizures
points.why: After a first seizure: urgent neurology clinic.

points.p: Abnormal electrical activity in the brain

prompts.q: Describe the main generalised seizure types.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the description of the event is the answer.

points.p: Tonic-clonic: stiffening then rhythmic jerking, eyes open, postictal confusion
Myoclonic: brief shock-like jerks, consciousness kept
Atonic: sudden loss of tone, drop attack
Absence: abrupt brief blank staring, normal between

prompts.q: How do temporal and frontal lobe focal seizures present?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: localise from the symptoms.

points.p: Temporal: epigastric aura, déjà vu, automatisms (lip-smacking)
points.why: Most common cause of complex partial seizures.

points.p: Temporal: postictal dysphasia, smell/taste hallucinations
Frontal: bizarre posturing, hyperkinetic, Jacksonian march
points.why: Clonic movement spreading up a limb.

points.p: Focal aware keeps awareness; impaired-awareness has no recollection

prompts.q: What is juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and what triggers it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: teenager, mornings, after a party.

points.p: Triad: myoclonic jerks, absences, GTCS
1 to 2 hours after waking
points.why: Dropping things at breakfast is the stem detail.

points.p: Triggered by sleep deprivation, alcohol, photic stimulation
points.why: Lifestyle advice is part of treatment.

prompts.q: How do you tell a seizure from a non-epileptic attack and from syncope?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: eyes, movements, duration and recovery.

points.p: NEAD: pelvic thrusting, mobile head, closed eyes, >3 minutes, weeping
points.why: More common in women, linked to stress or a family history of epilepsy.

points.p: Syncope: rapid recovery, short post-ictal period
points.why: A few jerks can occur in syncope.

points.p: Quinolones like ciprofloxacin lower the seizure threshold

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: glucose first in an active seizure.

points.p: Gold standard: clinical diagnosis supported by EEG
points.why: A normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy.

points.p: Bloods: glucose and electrolytes
Status: capillary glucose promptly
MRI brain for a structural cause
points.why: Second line once epilepsy is suspected.

prompts.q: How do you treat convulsive status epilepticus, step by step?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: check if IV access exists and how many doses are given.

points.p: IV lorazepam 4 mg, up to two doses
points.why: Prehospital: buccal midazolam or PR diazepam.

points.p: Then IV phenytoin, levetiracetam or valproate
points.why: Phenytoin also for uncontrolled seizures after head injury.

points.p: Refractory: ITU and general anaesthesia
Eclampsia: IV magnesium sulphate

prompts.q: Which AED is first line for each seizure type, and what happens after a first seizure?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: seizure type plus sex and age decide the drug.

points.p: First seizure: urgent outpatient neurology, discharge; no AED usually
points.why: AEDs only started before review in exceptional cases.

points.p: Focal and GTCS: lamotrigine or levetiracetam
Myoclonic: levetiracetam; avoid valproate in childbearing age
points.why: Valproate is avoided in both males and females of childbearing age.

points.p: Absence: ethosuximide

prompts.q: How is epilepsy managed long term, including pregnancy, withdrawal and side effects?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: valproate in a woman is the classic wrong answer.

points.p: Pregnancy: lamotrigine with 5 mg folic acid, avoid dual therapy
points.why: Phenytoin interferes with folate; breastfeeding is safe.

points.p: Consider withdrawal if seizure-free over 2 years, taper over 2 to 3 months
Lamotrigine: rash, Stevens-Johnson
Valproate: weight gain, teratogenic, tremor; topiramate: weight loss, stones
points.why: Phenytoin: gum hyperplasia, hirsutism, folate depletion.

points.p: Carbamazepine interacts with contraception: IUS preferred

prompts.q: How do the main AEDs work, and why does status get harder to treat with time?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: GABA-A for benzodiazepines, sodium channels for phenytoin and lamotrigine.

points.p: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A chloride influx
Phenytoin and lamotrigine block voltage-gated sodium channels
Valproate increases GABA and blocks Na/Ca channels
Prolonged status internalises GABA-A receptors
points.why: So benzodiazepines must be given early.

points.p: Temporal seizures often arise from mesial temporal sclerosis (hippocampus)

glossary.Epilepsy: A tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures, usually diagnosed after two or more.
glossary.Seizure: A burst of abnormal, hypersynchronous electrical activity in the brain causing symptoms.
glossary.GTCS: Generalised tonic-clonic seizure: stiffening then rhythmic jerking with loss of consciousness.
glossary.Tonic: The stiffening phase of a seizure, with sustained muscle contraction.
glossary.Clonic: The rhythmic jerking phase of a seizure.
glossary.Postictal: The recovery period after a seizure, often with confusion and drowsiness.
glossary.Aura: A warning sensation at the start of a focal seizure, such as an epigastric feeling.
glossary.Myoclonic: Brief, shock-like muscle jerks without loss of consciousness.
glossary.Atonic: A seizure with sudden loss of muscle tone causing a drop attack.
glossary.Absence: A brief generalised seizure with blank staring, typical in children.
glossary.Automatisms: Repetitive purposeless movements during a seizure, such as lip-smacking or fiddling.
glossary.Focal aware: A focal seizure where the person stays aware throughout.
glossary.Focal impaired-awareness: A focal seizure where awareness is lost and the person cannot recall it.
glossary.Jacksonian march: Clonic jerking that spreads up a limb, from a frontal motor cortex focus.
glossary.Todd's paresis: Temporary weakness of a limb after a focal motor seizure.
glossary.Déjà vu: A strong feeling of having lived a moment before; a temporal lobe aura.
glossary.JME: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: morning jerks, absences and GTCS in teenagers.
glossary.Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: A generalised epilepsy of adolescence with morning myoclonic jerks, absences and tonic-clonic seizures.
glossary.Mesial temporal sclerosis: Scarring of the hippocampus, a common cause of temporal lobe epilepsy.
glossary.NEAD: Non-epileptic attack disorder: seizure-like events with a psychological, not electrical, cause.
glossary.Non-epileptic attack disorder: Seizure-like attacks from psychological distress, with closed eyes and pelvic thrusting.
glossary.Syncope: A brief loss of consciousness from reduced brain blood flow, with rapid recovery.
glossary.Status epilepticus: A seizure lasting over 5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery in between.
glossary.EEG: Electroencephalogram: records the brain's electrical activity through scalp electrodes.
glossary.Lorazepam: A benzodiazepine given IV first line for status epilepticus.
glossary.Buccal midazolam: A benzodiazepine given inside the cheek when there is no IV access.
glossary.Phenytoin: A sodium channel blocking AED given IV as second line in status epilepticus.
glossary.Levetiracetam: A broad-spectrum AED, first choice for myoclonic seizures and safe in women.
glossary.Lamotrigine: A sodium channel blocking AED, preferred in pregnancy; can cause a serious rash.
glossary.Sodium valproate: A broad-spectrum AED that is highly teratogenic and avoided in women of childbearing age.
glossary.Ethosuximide: A T-type calcium channel blocker, first line for absence seizures.
glossary.Carbamazepine: A second-line AED for focal seizures; an enzyme inducer that weakens hormonal contraception.
glossary.Topiramate: An AED that causes weight loss, kidney stones and cognitive slowing.
glossary.Teratogenic: Able to cause birth defects when taken in pregnancy.
glossary.Stevens-Johnson syndrome: A rare, severe blistering skin and mucosal reaction to drugs such as lamotrigine.
glossary.Gum hyperplasia: Overgrowth of the gums, a side effect of long-term phenytoin.
glossary.GABA-A: The main inhibitory brain receptor; benzodiazepines boost its chloride current.
glossary.Hyperpolarisation: Making a neuron's inside more negative so it is less likely to fire.
glossary.Ketogenic diet: A high-fat, very low-carbohydrate diet that can reduce seizures in some patients.
glossary.Ciprofloxacin: A quinolone antibiotic that lowers the seizure threshold.
glossary.IUS: Intrauterine system (e.g. Mirena), the contraception of choice with enzyme-inducing AEDs.
glossary.Magnesium sulphate: The treatment for eclamptic seizures in pre-eclampsia.
glossary.DVLA: The UK Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency, which sets driving rules after seizures.
